item.title: Ill Bloom Crypto Wallet Drains and BlackCat Negotiator Sentencing
item.content:encoded:
Attackers Exploit 'Ill Bloom' Vulnerability to Drain $3.1 Million From Cryptocurrency Wallets — Must Read

Coinspect says attackers exploited the “Ill Bloom” weak-randomness flaw in some older or lesser-known crypto wallets to drain about $3.1 million from 431 wallets, with more funds potentially exposed. Users should check public addresses at illbloom.org and, if matched, move funds to a brand-new wallet with a freshly generated recovery phrase.

  • Coinspect disclosed a crypto wallet flaw called Ill Bloom, where some wallet software generated recovery phrases with weak randomness that attackers could work out.
  • Coinspect confirmed a coordinated sweep on May 27 that drained about $3.1 million from 431 wallets, with roughly $2 million more moving from exposed wallets since then.
  • Coinspect says wallets created on hardware devices are not affected, and most mainstream software wallets are not affected, while the real risk is with older or lesser-known mobile wallets, some dating back to 2018.
  • The affected weak phrases can expose funds across every chain they control, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Rootstock, Tron, and Polygon addresses traced by Coinspect.
  • Coinspect advises users to check public wallet addresses at illbloom.org and, if there is a match, create a brand-new wallet with a brand-new recovery phrase and move funds there.

Ransomware Negotiator Gets 70 Months in Prison for Aiding BlackCat Attacks — Should Read

Former ransomware negotiator Angelo Martino was sentenced to 70 months in U.S. prison for secretly helping BlackCat operators extort his own clients by sharing their confidential negotiation and insurance details. Prosecutors said he also helped target additional victims with two other cybersecurity professionals, while authorities have seized $10 million in illicit assets.

  • Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old former ransomware negotiator from Land O'Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in U.S. prison for conspiring with BlackCat ransomware operators to extort multiple victims.
  • Federal prosecutors said Martino worked as a negotiator for five ransomware victims while secretly giving BlackCat attackers confidential information about the victims' negotiation positions, strategies, and insurance policy limits.
  • Martino pleaded guilty in April to one count of conspiring to interfere with interstate commerce through extortion.
  • Martino was also accused of colluding with Ryan Goldberg and Kevin Martin to deploy BlackCat ransomware against multiple U.S. victims between April 2023 and November 2023.
  • The Justice Department said law enforcement has seized $10 million in assets from Martino, including digital currency, vehicles, a food truck, and a luxury fishing boat.

item.title: OpenMandriva Alleges Contributor Sabotage After Repository Deletions and Package Obsoletions
item.content:encoded:
OpenMandriva Linux says contributor tried to sabotage the project — May Read

OpenMandriva says a former contributor attempted to sabotage the Linux distribution by deleting GitHub repositories and pushing an empty package that could have disrupted GNOME and Cosmic desktop packages for users. The contributor denies intending harm, while the project is restoring affected repositories and auditing for further unauthorized changes.

  • The OpenMandriva Linux project said it was targeted by an attempted internal sabotage following a dispute among contributors.
  • OpenMandriva maintainer AngryPenguin said Davide Beatrici deleted part of a repository the team had worked on for almost a decade after previously receiving administrative privileges to help migrate and mirror repositories to his private OneDev instance.
  • AngryPenguin said Beatrici also published an empty package in the Cooker repository that obsoleted packages for the GNOME and Cosmic desktop environments.
  • The OpenMandriva team said it is restoring deleted repositories and packages and conducting a full system audit for other unauthorized changes.
  • Beatrici rejected the sabotage claims in a statement to The Lunduke Journal, saying he did not intend to harm OpenMandriva or its users.

item.title: Injective SDK, Braintree.Net Supply Chain Malware, GigaWiper, and UAT-7810 ORBs
item.content:encoded:
Injective SDK on npm infected with cryptocurrency wallet stealer — Should Read

Hackers compromised Injective Labs’ GitHub repository to publish malicious npm versions of its SDK and related packages that stole crypto wallet private keys and seed phrases when wallet functions were used. Developers who installed the affected version should assume wallets and secrets may be compromised, move funds to new wallets, and rotate credentials.

  • Hackers compromised a GitHub account belonging to a legitimate Injective Labs SDK project contributor and used it to publish malicious version 1.20.21 of the @injectivelabs/sdk-ts npm package.
  • The malicious package stole cryptocurrency wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases when developers used SDK functions that generate or import wallet keys.
  • The attacker also published version 1.20.21 for 17 other packages associated with the project, pinning all of them to the compromised SDK version.
  • Socket reported that the malicious package version was downloaded 310 times before it was deprecated, and Ox Security warned that 87 dependent packages had a cumulative download count of just over 112,000.
  • The legitimate account owner detected the compromise within minutes, reverted the changes, and published a clean release, version 1.20.23.

Fake Braintree NuGet Package Skims Credit Cards and Harvests Merchant Credentials — Should Read

A malicious NuGet typosquat, Braintree.Net, impersonated PayPal Braintree’s official SDK while stealing live payment card data, Braintree merchant API keys, and host secrets through a companion DependencyInjector.Core package. Any organization that used the affected packages should remove them, rotate credentials, investigate possible card-data exposure, and block the attacker domain.

  • Socket’s AI scanner flagged a malicious NuGet package named Braintree.Net that masqueraded as PayPal Braintree’s official .NET SDK and routed stolen data to api.348672-shakepay[.]com.
  • Confirmed malicious Braintree.Net versions 3.35.8 through 3.36.1 intercepted live payment card data, including full card numbers, CVVs, expiration dates, customer IDs, amounts, operations, gateways, card types, and timestamps.
  • The typosquat stole Braintree merchant credentials by sending merchantId, publicKey, and privateKey values to the attacker endpoint when a production gateway was configured.
  • Starting with Braintree.Net 3.36.0, the package depended on DependencyInjector.Core, which used module initializers to collect environment variables, appsettings JSON contents, cloud and container metadata, dependencies, and loaded assemblies on assembly load.
  • Socket recommended removing Braintree.Net, replacing it with the official Braintree package, rotating Braintree merchant credentials, auditing for DependencyInjector.Core, SipNet, and SipNet.OpenAI.Realtime, and hunting for outbound POSTs to api.348672-shakepay[.]com.

New GigaWiper Windows Backdoor Bundles Disk Wiping, Fake Ransomware, and Spyware — Should Read

Microsoft analyzed GigaWiper, a Windows backdoor also tracked as BLUERABBIT, that combines spying and remote-control features with multiple destructive wipers disguised partly as ransomware. Defenders should focus on early detection and offline backups because once deployed, the malware can irreversibly destroy systems rather than enable recovery or ransom payment.

  • Microsoft analyzed a destructive Windows backdoor called GigaWiper that combines three older destructive programs into operator-selectable commands.
  • The same malicious files are tracked by Binary Defense as BLUERABBIT, and both reports list the same four hashes and matching command servers.
  • GigaWiper can wipe the physical drive, run fake ransomware based on Crucio that encrypts files without saving a key, or overwrite the Windows drive using a Go rewrite of FlockWiper.
  • The backdoor can also take screenshots, record the screen, open a hidden VNC session, collect system details, manage programs and services, edit the registry, and wipe Windows event logs.
  • Microsoft recommends watching for signals such as a recurring OneDrive Update scheduled task, RabbitMQ or Redis traffic from ordinary desktops, and processes using takeown and icacls on Windows boot files outside maintenance windows.

Dormant GitHub Accounts Help Attackers Blend In While Mapping Corporate Orgs — Should Read

Datadog Security Labs warns that attackers are using years-old dormant GitHub “ghost” accounts and compromised tokens to quietly enumerate corporate GitHub orgs, repos, and users via the GitHub API. Most activity targets public data for reconnaissance, but some cases escalated to cloning private repositories.

  • Datadog Security Labs warned of several overlapping campaigns systematically enumerating corporate GitHub organizations, repositories, and user accounts through the GitHub API.
  • The operators use automated scraping tools with custom or legitimate-sounding user agents, GitHub “ghost” accounts that are often years old, and compromised OAuth tokens or personal access tokens from legitimate users.
  • More than 50 dormant accounts and dozens of legitimate accounts with exposed or compromised personal access tokens were used to facilitate the enumeration.
  • The GitHub “ghost” accounts were created two to five years ago and left inactive for long periods before being used to issue API traffic across multiple organizations.
  • Most activity involved public data, but Datadog confirmed a few scenarios where attackers went beyond enumeration and cloned a private repository belonging to a single organization.

WolfSSL, GeoVision, VTK vulnerabilities — Optional

Cisco Talos disclosed and coordinated patches for vulnerabilities in WolfSSL, GeoVision, and VTK-DICOM, including input validation, command injection, buffer overflow, privilege escalation, and authentication issues. The largest impact is GeoVision, with 14 advisories covering 37 CVEs.

  • Cisco Talos’ Vulnerability Discovery & Research team disclosed three vulnerabilities in WolfSSL, fourteen in GeoVision, and one in VTK-DICOM.
  • The vulnerabilities discussed in the article have been patched by their respective vendors in line with Cisco’s third-party vulnerability disclosure policy.
  • The WolfSSL issues include two improper input validation vulnerabilities, TALOS-2026-2409 and TALOS-2026-2410, and one integer underflow vulnerability, TALOS-2026-2408.
  • Talos released 14 advisories for GeoVision vulnerabilities, covering 37 CVEs across issues such as memory corruption, OS command injection, buffer overflows, privilege escalation, reflected XSS, insufficient encryption, and lack of authentication.
  • Talos found one VTK-DICOM vulnerability, TALOS-2026-2366, tracked as CVE-2026-22879, which is a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability.

Winning 54% of the time — Optional

Cisco Talos reports that China-nexus actor UAT-7810 is expanding covert Operational Relay Box networks by exploiting unpatched Ruckus and ASUS routers and deploying custom backdoors like LONGLEASH and DOGLEASH. Defenders should prioritize patching edge devices and monitoring for unusual proxying or unauthorized connections.

  • Cisco Talos reported that the China-nexus threat actor UAT-7810 is expanding its Operational Relay Box networks with a new suite of custom malware.
  • UAT-7810 exploits known vulnerabilities in unpatched Ruckus and ASUS routers to deploy tools including upgraded LONGLEASH and DOGLEASH backdoors.
  • Talos says UAT-7810 builds covert networks to provide infrastructure for other APT groups to launch attacks against high-value targets.
  • The article states that ORB networks allow secondary threat actors to mask their origins and route malicious traffic through seemingly innocuous nodes.
  • Defenders are advised to fully patch edge devices, particularly Ruckus and ASUS routers, and monitor for unusual proxying behavior or unauthorized connections.

Why Do F1 Teams Need Cybersecurity, and How Is AI Changing the Threat Landscape? — Optional

F1 teams face enterprise-grade cyber risks because their competitive advantage depends on fast-moving telemetry, software, partner access, and global operations. The article argues that AI is making phishing, deepfakes, and discovery faster for attackers, while zero trust and AI-driven security controls are needed to protect data, identities, vendors, and AI systems.

  • Formula 1 teams generate hundreds of gigabytes of telemetry across a race weekend, and this data moves between the car, garage, trackside systems, factory, and pit wall.
  • The article says F1 teams must protect live telemetry, proprietary software and analytics, business data, and global operations across more than 20 countries in a season.
  • Third-party vendors, suppliers, contractors, media, and sponsors can extend an F1 team’s attack surface because they may need temporary or integrated access to systems.
  • The article identifies IP theft, ransomware, and social engineering as key threats facing F1 teams, with race timing increasing pressure during outages.
  • The article states that AI can help attackers create convincing phishing content, deepfakes, and automated discovery campaigns, while also helping defenders baseline normal behavior and correlate risks.

item.title: Helix and Forg365 target Microsoft 365 as Injective npm backdoor hits crypto wallets
item.content:encoded:
Injective npm Supply Chain Attack: 18 Packages Backdoored to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys — Must Read

Attackers compromised a trusted Injective Labs developer account and published backdoored npm packages that stole wallet seed phrases and private keys during wallet creation or loading. Anyone who installed the affected 1.20.21 packages should treat touched wallet secrets as exposed and rotate funds to new wallets.

  • On July 8, 2026, attackers used access to a trusted developer's account to add a backdoor to Injective Labs' TypeScript SDK for the Injective blockchain.
  • The malicious code was disguised as key derivation telemetry and sent wallet recovery phrases or raw private keys to an attacker-controlled server when PrivateKey.fromMnemonic() or PrivateKey.fromHex() was called.
  • The malicious version 1.20.21 was published across 18 @injectivelabs packages, with 17 packages carrying risk because they pinned the backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts dependency exactly.
  • The npm provenance for the malicious release pointed to a GitHub Actions trusted-publishing workflow from the InjectiveLabs/injective-ts repository, and the commits were authored under the existing maintainer identity thomasRalee.
  • Injective Labs removed the payload, deprecated version 1.20.21, and republished clean version 1.20.23 across all 18 affected packages about 49 minutes after the malicious packages went live.

New Helix vishing group emerges in SharePoint data theft attacks — Must Read

A new extortion group called Helix is using vishing, device-code phishing, and MFA abuse to compromise Microsoft 365 accounts and steal data from SharePoint. ReliaQuest says the group’s SharePoint exfiltration patterns are its clearest fingerprint and recommends disabling device code authentication where possible.

  • A new data-extortion group called Helix is using vishing, device-code phishing, and MFA abuse to steal data from SharePoint environments.
  • Helix operators have impersonated employees' managers by name or caller ID spoofing to trick targets into device-code phishing schemes.
  • After gaining access, Helix quickly registers a new multi-factor authenticator app, enumerates SharePoint, and exfiltrates files.
  • ReliaQuest said Helix’s strongest technical fingerprint is automated SharePoint enumeration and collection from 179.43.185[.]230 using the python-requests/2.28.1 user-agent.
  • ReliaQuest believes Helix may be linked to ShinyHunters and BlackFile based on similar techniques and infrastructure, but it did not find a definitive connection.

npm 12 Disables Install Scripts by Default to Reduce Supply Chain Risk — Should Read

GitHub released npm 12 with install scripts, Git dependencies, and remote URL dependencies disabled by default to reduce supply chain risk. It is also phasing out 2FA-bypass granular access tokens for sensitive npm actions and direct publishing, pushing maintainers toward trusted publishing or human approval workflows.

  • GitHub announced the release of npm version 12 with install scripts disabled by default and deprecated granular access tokens designed to bypass two-factor authentication.
  • In npm 12, dependency lifecycle scripts and implicit node-gyp builds no longer run unless explicitly allowed, and Git dependencies or remote URL dependencies are no longer resolved unless explicitly allowed.
  • Users must run “npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending” to review and approve trusted scripts, then commit the resulting allowlist in the package.json file.
  • In early August 2026, npm granular access tokens configured to bypass two-factor authentication will no longer be able to perform sensitive account, package, and organization management actions.
  • In January 2027, npm granular access tokens will no longer be able to publish directly, and GitHub recommends moving automated publishing to trusted publishing using OIDC or staged publishing with human approval.

New Forg365 phishing platform uses AI to target Microsoft 365 accounts — Should Read

A new phishing-as-a-service platform called Forg365 targets Microsoft 365 accounts using device-code and adversary-in-the-middle phishing, with AI-generated lures and tools to maintain access by refreshing stolen cookies. Defenders should restrict device-code authentication, monitor Entra and mailbox activity, and revoke sessions quickly if compromise is suspected.

  • Forg365 is a phishing-as-a-service operation focused on stealing Microsoft 365 accounts by combining adversary-in-the-middle phishing, device-code phishing, and AI-assisted lure generation.
  • ZeroBEC researchers accessed the Forg365 dashboard, which supports creating phishing campaigns, managing phishing links, configuring OAuth apps and SMTP profiles, managing tokens, and generating phishing emails with AI.
  • Forg365 includes a browser extension called ForgCookie that refreshes Microsoft SSO cookies to help attackers maintain access to Microsoft services linked to compromised accounts.
  • The platform supports device-code phishing that tricks victims into authorizing an attacker-controlled device through Microsoft’s legitimate OAuth 2.0 device code flow.
  • ZeroBEC recommends restricting or disabling Microsoft device-code authentication unless required, monitoring Microsoft Entra logs, investigating unexpected mailbox rules and OAuth grants, and revoking tokens and sessions if compromise is suspected.

Latvian forestry company still restoring systems weeks after ransomware attack — Should Read

Latvia’s state-owned forestry company LVM is still restoring systems weeks after a ransomware attack that disrupted services and exposed stolen data, including internal documents, credentials, certificates and code. CERT.LV attributed the incident to an unnamed foreign financially motivated ransomware group and said Latvia’s election infrastructure was not compromised.

  • Latvia's state-owned forestry company LVM is still working to restore IT systems weeks after a ransomware attack disrupted internal and customer services.
  • The attack knocked LVM's mapping platform, hunting application, and systems used to exchange information with contractors and customers offline.
  • LVM's chief technology officer said about two-thirds of customers with service contracts still do not have access to the affected systems.
  • CERT.LV attributed the intrusion to a foreign, financially motivated ransomware group and said the attackers leaked roughly 44 gigabytes of stolen data online.
  • Latvian authorities said election infrastructure was not compromised because the voter registration software was developed in a separate environment and its code was never stored in LVM's corporate repositories.

Microsoft expects more Windows security updates from AI-discovered flaws — May Read

Microsoft says its growing use of AI to find and validate Windows vulnerabilities will likely lead to more security fixes in monthly Patch Tuesday updates. The company says human engineers will still review fixes, while it also updates its development practices for AI-enabled attack techniques.

  • Microsoft says Windows users should expect more security updates as the company increasingly uses artificial intelligence to discover vulnerabilities in its codebase.
  • Microsoft is using Microsoft Security's multi-model agentic scanning harness, known as MDASH, to scan critical Windows binaries and validate potential vulnerabilities using multiple AI models.
  • Vulnerability candidates found by MDASH go through a Windows-specific validation pipeline to reduce false positives before engineers investigate them.
  • Microsoft says human engineers will oversee and review all proposed code and validate fixes before they are released into production.
  • Microsoft is updating its Secure Development Lifecycle practices to account for AI-enabled attack techniques and to use AI earlier in software development.

Finding SOCKS with Proxywatch — May Read

SpecterOps released ProxyWatch, a proof-of-concept tool that detects SOCKS proxy pivots, C2 sessions, and beaconing by analyzing endpoint behavior rather than relying on static indicators or process-port baselines. The key takeaway is that proxy-based attacker activity can be detected more reliably by profiling how processes communicate and relay traffic.

  • Adversaries use SOCKS proxy tunnels to pivot within environments and execute code against compromised systems without bringing tools to those systems.
  • SpecterOps created ProxyWatch as a proof-of-concept tool to detect SOCKS proxies and other pivoting methods through behavior-based detection.
  • ProxyWatch collects endpoint telemetry on Linux and Windows, including network, user, and process context, then scores processes using behavioral signals to assign roles such as C2 session, SOCKS proxy pivot, or beaconing behavior.
  • ProxyWatch includes a local machine learning model that reads 122 features per process and trains against the rule engine’s output while the rules provide detections from day one.
  • The article shows ProxyWatch detecting a Sliver Beacon SOCKS tunnel, a Sliver C2 beacon callback pattern, BloodHound-style relationship collection through ProxyHound, and egress paths through Contour.

Unmasking BitRAT's C2 over HTTPS | Corelight — May Read

Corelight analyzes how BitRAT hides command-and-control traffic inside HTTPS and shows that network telemetry can still expose its distinctive C2 behavior. The key takeaway is that encrypted malware traffic can often be detected through protocol metadata and traffic patterns rather than payload inspection.

  • The article is titled “Unmasking BitRAT's C2 over HTTPS.”
  • The article focuses on BitRAT.
  • The article discusses BitRAT command-and-control activity over HTTPS.
  • The article is associated with Corelight.

The Hidden Security Risks of Reduced Summer IT Coverage — Optional

Reduced summer IT staffing gives attackers more time to exploit phishing, unpatched systems, and delayed response processes. Organizations can reduce this risk by using automation, monitoring, and AI-driven alert prioritization to maintain security coverage when key staff are away.

  • Cybercriminals exploit summer vacation periods because reduced IT and security staffing can lead to slower response times and less oversight.
  • The article cites data indicating a 40% increase in cyberattacks during holiday periods, with summer months described as particularly vulnerable.
  • Lean staffing can make phishing and Business Email Compromise harder to spot, especially when approval chains are disrupted and key decision makers are out of the office.
  • Manual security processes such as ticket triage, threat investigations, patch deployment, and containment actions can become bottlenecks when staffing levels are reduced.
  • The article argues that AI-driven automation, automated patching, alert prioritization, runbook execution, and continuous monitoring can help maintain security coverage during staffing shortages.

Mitiga Joins Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program — Optional

Mitiga has joined Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program to use Claude’s advanced, vetted cyber reasoning for legitimate defensive work, especially improving runtime detections against AI-speed attacker tradecraft. The main takeaway is that as exploits increasingly outpace patches, Mitiga argues defenders need runtime controls that detect and stop attacks in progress, not just faster vulnerability remediation.

  • Mitiga has joined Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program so it can use Claude’s advanced cyber reasoning for legitimate defensive work that is normally blocked by default.
  • Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program unlocks certain dual-use activities, such as exploitation analysis, adversarial simulation, and threat modeling, for verified organizations while keeping activities such as ransomware code and mass data theft blocked for everyone.
  • The article argues that AI has compressed attackers’ timelines so much that exploitation can happen before patches are available, making patching alone insufficient.
  • Mitiga says verified access will help improve detections in Helios AIDR and Agentic Runtime Security by applying frontier-model reasoning to real attacker tradecraft.
  • The article presents Agentic Runtime Security as a compensating control that watches cloud, SaaS, identity, AI, and third-party services to detect, interrupt, and stop attacks before they cause business impact.

ThreatsDay: Cloud Bucket Hijacking, Windows LPE Chain, Global Fraud Bust + 17 More Stories — Optional

This week’s threats show how ordinary operational gaps—reused cloud bucket names, trusted remote tools, typosquatted packages, stale credentials, and loose egress controls—can quickly become paths for data theft, privilege escalation, and ransomware. The key takeaway is to scrutinize normal-looking workflows and permissions before attackers turn them into quiet compromise channels.

  • Operation First Light 2026 involved 97 countries and territories, led to 5,811 arrests, intercepted $293 million in illicit assets, and identified more than 142,000 victims of social engineering scams and related money laundering.
  • Seventeen malicious npm and PyPI packages typosquatted Paysafe, Skrill, and Neteller SDKs to steal system information and developer secrets and send them to an Ngrok endpoint.
  • A critical Esri ArcGIS Server flaw, CVE-2026-9181, could allow unauthenticated attackers to access sensitive files by using crafted path parameters in the REST Uploads resource.
  • A fake IT support campaign used phishing emails and Microsoft Teams calls to get victims to install remote access tools and ultimately deliver EtherRAT.
  • Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 described a cloud bucket hijacking technique in which an attacker can recreate a deleted globally unique bucket name under their own account and reroute logs or sensitive data to their environment.

item.title: GodDamn Ransomware, NIS2 Enforcement, and Cloudflare's Post-Quantum Signature Push
item.content:encoded:
GodDamn Ransomware Uses PoisonX Driver to Disable Endpoint Defenses — Must Read

A new GodDamn ransomware campaign, believed to be a rebrand of Beast/Monster, is using the Microsoft-signed PoisonX kernel driver in BYOVD attacks to disable endpoint defenses before encryption. The attackers also use AnyDesk, credential harvesting tools, PsExec, and PowerShell to move laterally and maintain access across victim networks.

  • Symantec researchers reported a new ransomware family called GodDamn that uses the PoisonX kernel driver to neutralize security software as part of its defense evasion strategy.
  • GodDamn was first publicly spotted in the wild on May 21, 2026, and Symantec assesses it to be a rebrand of Beast ransomware, which was an enhanced version of Monster ransomware.
  • In an early June 2026 attack, the threat actors used AnyDesk for remote access and a NirSoft-based credential harvesting toolkit before deploying the ransomware, while the initial access vector remained unknown.
  • The attack used a tool named symantec.exe and the PoisonX driver file g11.sys to disable endpoint defenses in a bring your own vulnerable driver attack.
  • The attackers used PsExec for lateral movement and installed AnyDesk as an auto-start Windows service across at least 10 hosts within the targeted organization by the end of June 2.

NSA revives 'Tailored Access Operations' name for elite hacking unit — Should Read

The NSA has renamed its elite hacking division back to Tailored Access Operations as part of a leadership-driven reorganization meant to strengthen offensive cyber operations against threats from countries like China and Russia. The move restores a historically significant unit known for custom intrusion tools and past involvement in operations such as Stuxnet.

  • The National Security Agency changed the name of its Office of Computer Network Operations back to Tailored Access Operations last week.
  • The renaming is part of a reorganization by NSA leadership intended to make the agency more adept at facing evolving digital threats from China, Russia, and others.
  • The change partly reverses the 2016 NSA21 restructuring, which had folded offensive operations and intelligence collection into broader directorates instead of keeping Tailored Access Operations as a standalone office.
  • Tailored Access Operations makes and deploys custom tools to penetrate foreign computer networks for espionage purposes and helped craft Stuxnet, which was used to sabotage Iran’s nuclear program.
  • The unit gained public attention after the Shadow Brokers advertised stolen NSA hacking techniques, including tools later linked to global attacks such as WannaCry using EternalBlue.

EU takes member states to court over unimplemented cybersecurity law — Should Read

The European Commission is taking Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the EU’s top court for failing to implement the NIS2 cybersecurity directive, seeking financial penalties until they comply. The law sets baseline security and incident-reporting rules for critical sectors such as hospitals, energy, transport and public administration.

  • The European Commission filed legal referrals at the Court of Justice of the European Union against Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands for failing to implement the NIS2 Directive.
  • Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands are more than 20 months late in transposing NIS2, which sets minimum security standards for critical infrastructure such as hospitals, energy networks, transport operators and public administrations.
  • The Commission asked the court to impose a lump sum and ongoing daily financial penalties on all four countries until each formally notifies full transposition.
  • ENISA warned of thousands of cybersecurity incidents affecting the EU in the year ending June 2025, with public administration identified as the most-targeted critical sector at 38% of incidents.
  • NIS2 widens the scope of the original 2016 Network and Information Security Directive to 18 critical sectors and adds risk management and incident reporting requirements.

The Compliance Notice That Borrowed the Government's Words and the Carrier's Own DOT Number — May Read

A carrier received a convincing fake FMCSA compliance notice that used its real USDOT number and legitimate regulatory language to push paid filing links for a free MCS-150 update. The key warning is that real public identifiers and accurate government terminology do not prove legitimacy; verify regulatory notices directly through official portals.

  • A logistics carrier received an email titled “Required FMCSA Biennial Update” that included the carrier’s genuine USDOT number and warned about fines and deactivation.
  • The email sold paid two-year, four-year, and lifetime registration tiers for an MCS-150 update that can be completed for free at the official FMCSA portal.
  • The sender used the domain dotregistrationsfirm.com, which was registered through GoDaddy in August 2023 and included a footer disclaimer stating it was not the Department of Transportation, the FMCSA, or any government agency.
  • Investigators found weak or inconsistent email authentication signals, including DMARC set to p=none for the visible sender domain and DKIM verifying at one hop but failing at the final receiver.
  • The article says behavioral analysis flagged the mismatch between the sender brand and link destinations, the urgency around fines and deactivation, and the payment request before any payment was made.

Microsoft to retire the OWA Light client in Exchange Server — May Read

Microsoft plans to disable and remove the legacy OWA Light client from on-premises Exchange Server in an upcoming update, likely in August 2026. Users will need to use the modern Outlook on the web experience, while admins can proactively block OWA Light now via Exchange PowerShell settings.

  • Microsoft announced plans to disable and remove OWA Light from Exchange Server in an upcoming update estimated for August 2026.
  • OWA Light was introduced roughly two decades ago as a simplified alternative for systems without Internet Explorer 6 or later, older browsers, low-bandwidth connections, or locked-down browser modes such as kiosks.
  • Microsoft said retiring OWA Light will reduce legacy surface area, simplify engineering work, and allow it to focus on the full Outlook on the web experience.
  • After the change is introduced, users will no longer be able to choose or be redirected to OWA Light and should use the modern Outlook on the web experience instead.
  • Admins can block OWA Light immediately with Set-OwaMailboxPolicy -OwaLightEnabled $false and remove the light selection menu on the logon page with Set-OwaVirtualDirectory -LogonPageLightSelectionEnabled $false.

Why we cannot wait for better post-quantum signature algorithms — Optional

Cloudflare argues organizations cannot wait for newer, smaller post-quantum signature schemes because they likely will not be standardized and broadly deployable until the 2030s. ML-DSA is imperfect but available now, so it should be used for the first migration while research continues on better alternatives.

  • Cloudflare says RSA and ECC are vulnerable to sufficiently advanced quantum computers, and it is targeting 2029 to become fully post-quantum secure.
  • The article states that ML-KEM encryption is already protecting the majority of traffic handled by Cloudflare, while post-quantum signatures are still needed to secure authentication systems against quantum-capable attackers.
  • ML-DSA is described as the best all-around post-quantum signature scheme standardized today, but it has larger public keys and signatures than classical schemes and lacks some capabilities available with RSA and ECC.
  • NIST has advanced nine post-quantum signature schemes to the third round of its signatures on-ramp, but the article argues that these schemes will not be ready in time for the first post-quantum migration.
  • The article concludes that organizations should not wait for future signature algorithms, because deploying post-quantum signatures and handling downgrade risks will require a long transition period.

Summer of Clearinghouses — Optional

Chainguard argues that the real value of new open source vulnerability clearinghouses is not collecting private findings, but rapidly turning them into rebuilt, tested, signed fixes and upstream patches. The clearinghouses that matter will be the few that can orchestrate fixes at scale, measure throughput and reach, and ultimately help move the ecosystem toward secure-by-design software.

  • Chainguard says its clearinghouse, Athena, was built and operating months before it was announced, taking vulnerability findings and shipping fixes for customers.
  • The article argues that a clearinghouse is only a pool of vulnerability data, and the more important capability is turning findings into rebuilt, tested, signed artifacts that users can consume.
  • Chainguard says its build system watches thousands of open source projects, rebuilds from source, tests, and signs fixes when advisories land, with most CVEs remediated in roughly two days.
  • The article says new private vulnerability findings are increasing because models are being used against running applications and often discover flaws in open source dependencies rather than only first-party code.
  • The article argues that successful clearinghouses should be judged by median time from finding to shipped fix, the fraction handled without human intervention, and the share of fixes that land upstream.

Introducing the Risk Score Engine: identity risk you can quantify — Optional

Permiso has launched its Risk Score Engine, which assigns continuous 0–100 identity risk scores across human, non-human, and AI identities. The platform breaks scores into behavior, likelihood, and impact dimensions and rolls them up into organization-level risk metrics.

  • Permiso is launching the Risk Score Engine, which assigns every identity in an environment a continuous, evidence-backed score from 0 to 100.
  • The Risk Score Engine breaks every score down across Behavior, Likelihood, and Impact dimensions so identities with the same score can still require different responses.
  • The scores are built on Permiso’s Universal Identity Graph and cover human, non-human, and AI identities.
  • Score velocity tracks how fast a score is moving because the article says rate of change is often the earliest sign something is wrong.
  • The engine produces Identity Risk Scores, Session Scores, and Organization Risk Scores, with organization scores benchmarked against peers.

AI Attacks Move in Minutes. Join This Webinar on Building a Defense That Keeps Up — Optional

AI-powered attacks can move from phishing to lateral movement in minutes, outpacing traditional network-based defenses. The webinar will show how Zero Trust, least privilege, and automated containment can help teams reduce exposure and stop attacks earlier.

  • The article says AI has changed attack speed by letting attackers perform work that once took days in minutes.
  • The article states that attackers using models like Mythos can write tailored bait, pick targets, test what works, and move to the next host before a team clears the first alert.
  • The free webinar, titled "Outpacing Mythos: How to Fight Back Against AI-Powered Attacks," will explain how AI-powered attacks get in, what they do once inside, and why network-based defenses can fall behind.
  • The webinar will present three defensive moves: shrinking what attackers can reach, stopping lateral movement by design, and using tripwires to trigger automated containment.
  • Zscaler's Olivia Vort will show how to apply a Zero Trust approach intended to respond at machine speed.

item.title: Operation First Light 2026, AssuranceAmerica Breach, and Meta AI Permission Risks
item.content:encoded:
AssuranceAmerica data breach exposes records of 6.9 million drivers — Must Read

AssuranceAmerica disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 7 million drivers after attackers accessed its IT systems and stole files containing personal, policy, vehicle, claims, and driver’s license information. The company says it has contained the intrusion, strengthened security measures, and is notifying affected individuals.

  • AssuranceAmerica disclosed in a filing with Maine's Office of the Attorney General that a data breach exposed information belonging to 6,998,886 people.
  • AssuranceAmerica detected suspicious activity on March 17, 2026, and determined that malicious activity on March 16, 2026 targeted one of its employees.
  • The company said an unauthorized third party accessed parts of its IT environment and copied certain data files.
  • The stolen documents contained combinations of names, contact information, automobile insurance policy or account information, driver or vehicle information, claims-related information, and driver's license numbers.
  • AssuranceAmerica said it disabled compromised credentials and unauthorized sessions, isolated affected systems, notified law enforcement, reset passwords, deployed enhanced monitoring and threat detection tools, and provided additional cybersecurity instruction to personnel.

Police arrests 5,800 suspects in global anti-fraud crackdown — Should Read

INTERPOL-coordinated Operation First Light 2026 led to 5,811 arrests across 97 countries and the seizure of $293 million tied to social engineering fraud and money laundering. Authorities identified over 142,000 victims and blocked more than 31,000 bank accounts, underscoring the global scale of cyber-enabled financial scams.

  • Law enforcement agencies arrested 5,811 suspects and seized $293 million in illicit assets during Operation First Light 2026, a global anti-fraud operation spanning 97 countries.
  • Operation First Light 2026 targeted social engineering fraud, including business email compromise, sextortion, impersonation, romance, and investment scams, as well as money laundering activities between January 15 and April 30.
  • Investigators identified more than 142,000 victims worldwide, blocked 31,014 bank accounts, analyzed 152,808 cases, and identified 15,606 additional suspects beyond those arrested.
  • The operation was coordinated by INTERPOL, funded by China’s Ministry of Public Security, and supported by ASEANAPOL, GCCPOL, and Europol.
  • INTERPOL said the operation included action against high-value targets, raids on identified premises, blocking or freezing bank accounts and virtual wallets, and use of its Global Rapid Intervention of Payments stop-payment mechanism.

Meta's New AI Image Tool Lets Others Use Your Public Instagram Photos in AI Images — May Read

Meta’s new Muse Image AI feature lets users generate images using public Instagram posts and reels by tagging accounts, and the reuse setting is enabled by default. Public Instagram users who don’t want their content used this way should disable content reuse in Instagram settings.

  • Meta announced that its Muse Image AI model lets people use public Instagram posts and reels to generate AI content, and the feature is enabled by default.
  • Users can @-mention public Instagram accounts in the Meta AI app so Meta AI can use public photos to create images for posts, reels, stories, invitations, graphics, or other visual content.
  • Instagram users are not notified when their images are reused through Meta’s AI features, although notifications still apply for remixes, sequences, stickers, and templates.
  • Meta says public Instagram users can disable this reuse by going to Instagram settings, opening Sharing and reuse, and turning off reuse for Posts and Reels.
  • The article says the feature is part of a broader trend in which companies such as Meta and Google are adding AI-related data use settings that are opt-out rather than opt-in by default.

AI Authority Drift: The Permissions Nobody Approved — Optional

AI agents are accumulating permissions through integrations and inherited access faster than traditional reviews can track, creating “authority drift” that attackers can exploit using the agents’ own legitimate access. Organizations need live visibility and real-time enforcement of agent permissions rather than relying on static approval records or periodic reviews.

  • The article defines authority drift as an AI agent’s permission footprint expanding beyond what was originally approved until nobody can account for everything it can reach.
  • The article says AI agent access grows through inherited permissions from connected systems, new integrations added to solve immediate problems, and broad access granted for convenience.
  • In September 2025, state-sponsored attackers hijacked enterprise AI agent instances across 30 targets in defense, energy, and technology, using the agents’ accumulated access to move laterally in minutes.
  • CVE-2025-32711 was described as a zero-click prompt injection in Microsoft 365 Copilot that used a crafted email to extract data from OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams through a trusted Microsoft domain.
  • The article argues that organizations need a live map of each agent’s access, restrictions to a fixed set of tools or models, and an enforcement point that can scope access without waiting for the next scheduled review.

item.title: RoguePlanet Defender zero-day patched as AI coding agents face Friendly Fire and GhostApproval flaws
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft patches RoguePlanet Defender zero-day vulnerability — Must Read

Microsoft has patched the RoguePlanet zero-day in Microsoft Defender, tracked as CVE-2026-50656, via a Malware Protection Engine update. The flaw could let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges on fully patched Windows 10 and 11 systems using a race condition exploit.

  • Microsoft released a security patch for a Microsoft Defender zero-day vulnerability known as RoguePlanet, tracked as CVE-2026-50656.
  • The vulnerability was disclosed by a security researcher using the handle Nightmare Eclipse, who also shared a proof-of-concept exploit in a self-hosted Git repository.
  • Nightmare Eclipse said RoguePlanet affects fully patched Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices and can allow attackers to spawn a command prompt with SYSTEM privileges via a Microsoft Defender race condition.
  • Microsoft addressed the RoguePlanet vulnerability by releasing Microsoft Malware Protection Engine version 1.1.26060.3008.
  • Nightmare Eclipse has disclosed multiple other Windows zero-day exploits in recent months, including flaws affecting Microsoft Defender, BitLocker, and other Windows components.

Fake 7-Zip Installers Turn Devices Into Residential Proxy Nodes — Must Read

Researchers say a China-based actor dubbed Lurking Lizard has used fake 7-Zip installers, lookalike domains, and fake proxy-service brands to covertly turn victims’ devices into residential proxy nodes. The operation appears to be a full proxy-business ecosystem spanning victim recruitment, infrastructure, marketing, and monetization.

  • Infoblox researchers disclosed that a threat actor dubbed Lurking Lizard has operated a malicious residential proxy business using more than 230 lookalike domains since at least August 2022.
  • One campaign used a trojanized 7-Zip installer hosted on the lookalike domain 7zip[.]com to covertly recruit compromised devices as proxy nodes.
  • Lurking Lizard has impersonated major proxy providers including IPIDEA, SmartProxy, IP Royal, and 911Proxy, and has run fake independent review sites to direct traffic to its scam storefronts.
  • WHOIS analysis and infrastructure fingerprinting suggest that Lurking Lizard is a China-based actor, and the campaign has also used popular VPNs and services like HeroSMS as decoys to distribute proxy malware.
  • Infoblox said the operation spans victim acquisition, proxy infrastructure, marketing, and monetization, turning recruited devices into a pool that can be sold through lookalike proxy service brands.

GhostApproval Symlink Flaws Could Let Malicious Repos Run Code in AI Coding Agents — Should Read

Wiz researchers found that several AI coding assistants can be tricked by malicious repositories into writing through symlinks to sensitive files like SSH keys or shell startup scripts, while approval prompts show only harmless-looking paths. Some vendors have patched the issue, but users should update tools and avoid running agents on untrusted repos without sandboxing or limiting file access.

  • Wiz researchers identified a GhostApproval flaw in six AI coding assistants: Amazon Q Developer, Anthropic's Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf.
  • The attack uses a malicious repository with a symbolic link, such as a project_settings.json file that actually points to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, causing an assistant-approved write to modify a sensitive file instead.
  • Wiz found that approval dialogs can show the harmless-looking symlink path rather than the real file being modified, creating what it calls an informed-consent bypass.
  • As of publication, Amazon Q Developer, Cursor, and Google Antigravity had shipped fixes, Augment and Windsurf had acknowledged the issue without fixes, and Anthropic disputed that Claude Code behavior was a bug.
  • Wiz recommended that tool makers resolve symlinks and show the true destination before asking for approval, flag writes outside the project folder, and avoid touching disk before the user approves.

Top AI Agents Built to Catch Malicious Code Can Be Tricked Into Running It — Should Read

AI Now researchers showed that autonomous AI coding agents like Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can be tricked by instructions in a repository README into running malicious scripts while reviewing untrusted code. The key takeaway is that agents with command execution should not be used on untrusted projects without strict human approval and isolation, because model safety checks are not reliable containment.

  • AI Now Institute researchers published a proof-of-concept called Friendly Fire showing that Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex can be tricked into running attacker-controlled code when autonomous command-approval modes are enabled.
  • The tested setups included Claude Code CLI versions 2.1.116, 2.1.196, 2.1.198, and 2.1.199 on Claude Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, or Opus 4.8, and OpenAI Codex CLI 0.142.4 on GPT-5.5.
  • The demo placed extra files in the geopy Python library, used a README note to suggest running security.sh, and had that script quietly launch a hidden binary carrying the real payload.
  • The researchers said there is no patch to wait for because the weakness is in the workflow design, where agents cannot reliably separate untrusted repository text from instructions they should follow.
  • The article states there is no reported exploitation in the wild, the public GitHub code has the payload stripped, and the proof-of-concept stops at initial code execution without privilege escalation or lateral movement.
